People Who Never Reached Age 33

Alexander the Great

Birth date: July 19, 357 BCE

Death date: June 9, 324 BCE

Age: 32

Alexander the Great, king of Macedon and one of antiquity’s most influential commanders, inherited the throne at 20 and built an empire stretching from Greece through Egypt and Persia toward northwestern India. Undefeated in battle, he spread Greek political and cultural influence across much of the ancient world. He died in Babylon in June 323 BCE after a sudden illness, before securing a clear succession, leaving his empire to fragment among his generals. He was 32.

Bruce Lee

Birth date: November 26, 1940

Death date: July 19, 1973

Age: 32

Bruce Lee, born Lee Jun-fan, was a Hong Kong and American martial artist, actor, filmmaker, and founder of Jeet Kune Do. Through films such as The Big Boss, Fist of Fury, The Way of the Dragon, and Enter the Dragon, he became the first global Chinese film star and transformed martial-arts cinema worldwide. He died suddenly in Hong Kong on 1973-07-20 at the age of 32 after collapsing into a coma; cerebral edema is commonly cited, while the exact cause remains debated.

Srinivasa Ramanujan

Birth date: December 21, 1887

Death date: April 25, 1920

Age: 32

Srinivasa Ramanujan was an Indian mathematician whose extraordinary intuition transformed number theory, infinite series, continued fractions, partitions, and modular forms. Largely self-taught, he developed thousands of identities and formulas, many later proved correct and influential. His correspondence with G. H. Hardy brought him to Cambridge, where his originality astonished leading mathematicians. In 1919, worsening illness forced him to return to India; he died in Kumbakonam on 26 April 1920, aged 32, while still producing new mathematical ideas.

Franz Schubert

Birth date: January 30, 1797

Death date: November 18, 1828

Age: 31

Franz Peter Schubert was an Austrian composer who helped bridge the late Classical and early Romantic eras. Celebrated for his gift for melody, he wrote more than a thousand works, including hundreds of Lieder, major chamber music, piano works, masses, and symphonies such as the Unfinished Symphony. His music became far more widely admired after his death. Schubert died in Vienna on 19 November 1828 at the age of 31; the official diagnosis was typhoid fever, though later writers have discussed other possible causes.

Nero

Birth date: December 14, 37

Death date: June 8, 68

Age: 30
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Nero is one of the most notorious Roman emperors. His reputation is tied to political executions, alleged cruelty, persecution of Christians, violence within his own family, and the disputed but enduring association with the Great Fire of Rome. Some ancient accounts are hostile and partly propagandistic, but his public image remains strongly associated with tyranny and brutality.

Nero was the fifth Roman emperor and the last ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, reigning from AD 54 to 68. Remembered for his theatrical tastes, ambitious building projects, political violence, and the controversies surrounding the Great Fire of Rome, he remains one of antiquity’s most notorious rulers. Facing rebellion, abandonment by key supporters, and condemnation by the Senate, Nero fled Rome and died by suicide on 9 June AD 68 at the age of 30.

Jim Morrison

Birth date: December 7, 1943

Death date: July 2, 1971

Age: 27

Jim Morrison was an American singer, songwriter, and poet, best known as the charismatic lead vocalist and chief lyricist of The Doors. With songs such as "Light My Fire," "Break on Through," and "Riders on the Storm," he became one of the defining voices of late-1960s rock and counterculture, admired for his dark poetic lyrics, powerful stage presence, and rebellious image. In 1971, after moving to Paris, he died unexpectedly in an apartment at the age of 27; because no autopsy was performed, the exact cause of death has remained disputed, which only deepened the legend surrounding him.

Death date: July 7, 1822

Age: 29

Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the great English Romantic poets, remembered for works such as “Ozymandias,” “Ode to the West Wind,” “To a Skylark,” and Prometheus Unbound. Brilliant, radical, and often controversial, he challenged political, religious, and social conventions and became far more influential after his lifetime. In 1822, while living in Italy, he drowned when his small sailing boat was caught in stormy weather on a return voyage from Livorno to Lerici. He was 29.

Emily Brontë

Birth date: July 29, 1818

Death date: December 18, 1848

Age: 30

Emily Jane Brontë was an English novelist and poet, best remembered for her only novel, Wuthering Heights, a fierce and atmospheric classic of English literature published under the pen name Ellis Bell. Raised in the Yorkshire village of Haworth with her literary siblings Charlotte and Anne, she lived a largely private life shaped by the moors, family imagination, and intense creative discipline. Her health declined rapidly in 1848, soon after the death of her brother Branwell; she refused medical help until it was too late and died of tuberculosis in Haworth at the age of 30.

Birth date: August 30, 12

Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Caligula is one of the most notorious Roman emperors. Ancient sources portray him as cruel, arbitrary, sexually abusive, financially exploitative, and willing to use executions and humiliation to consolidate personal power. Modern historians debate how much of this reputation comes from hostile elite sources, but his public image remains strongly associated with tyranny and abuse.

Caligula, born Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, was the third Roman emperor, ruling from 37 to 41 CE; remembered for his volatile reputation, concentration of imperial power, and ambitious public works, he remains one of antiquity’s most debated rulers. In January 41 he was assassinated at the Palatine Games in a conspiracy led by Praetorian officers, ending his reign at age 28.

Birth date: December 31, 84 BCE

Death date: December 31, 54 BCE

Age: 30

Gaius Valerius Catullus was one of the sharpest and most personal poets of the late Roman Republic, famous for intense love poems, polished insults, and the emotionally charged figure of Lesbia. Born in Verona and active in Rome, he helped define the neoteric style of Latin poetry. He died young in Rome around 54 BCE, probably at about 30; no reliable ancient account records the medical cause or precise circumstances of his death.

Spartacus

Birth date: December 31, 103 BCE

Death date: March 31, 71 BCE

Age: 32

Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator who became the most famous leader of the Third Servile War, the major slave uprising against the Roman Republic from 73 to 71 BC. After escaping a gladiatorial school near Capua, he helped turn a small band of fugitives into a powerful rebel force that defeated several Roman armies. His life is known mostly from later writers such as Plutarch and Appian, and he became an enduring symbol of resistance against oppression. In 71 BC, his army was finally defeated by forces under Marcus Licinius Crassus; Spartacus is believed to have been killed in the final battle, though his body was never identified.

Richard III of England

Birth date: October 1, 1452

Death date: August 21, 1485

Age: 32
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Richard III remains one of England’s most disputed monarchs. His seizure of the throne after the young Edward V and his brother were declared illegitimate, the unresolved disappearance of the Princes in the Tower, and later Tudor and Shakespearean portrayals made him a lasting symbol of suspected usurpation and political murder, even though modern historians debate how much blame is justified.

Richard III of England was the last king of the House of York and the final Plantagenet monarch, ruling from 1483 to 1485 during the turbulent Wars of the Roses. Brother of Edward IV, he became king after the young Edward V and his brother were declared illegitimate, a controversy tied forever to the mystery of the Princes in the Tower. Richard died aged 32 at the Battle of Bosworth Field, where Henry Tudor defeated him and founded the Tudor dynasty as Henry VII.

Christopher Marlowe, also known as Kit Marlowe, was one of the defining voices of Elizabethan drama: a playwright, poet, translator, and major predecessor of Shakespeare. Commodus was a Roman emperor, the son of Marcus Aurelius, who ruled first as co-emperor and then alone from 180 to 192. His reign is often remembered as a turning point after the stability of the Pax Romana, marked by court intrigue, autocratic rule, and his notorious public performances as a gladiator. In late 192, after a conspiracy formed around members of his inner circle, he was first poisoned unsuccessfully and then strangled by the wrestler Narcissus, dying in Rome at the age of 31.

Caracalla

Birth date: April 3, 188

Death date: April 7, 217

Age: 29
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Caracalla is a highly controversial Roman emperor, strongly associated with autocratic brutality. Ancient and modern accounts link him to the murder of his brother Geta, a purge of Geta's supporters, severe political violence, and the alleged massacre of people in Alexandria.

Caracalla, born Lucius Septimius Bassianus and later known as Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, was a Severan Roman emperor and the son of Septimius Severus and Julia Domna. He ruled first alongside his father, briefly with his brother Geta, and then alone after Geta’s murder. His reign is remembered for the Antonine Constitution, which extended Roman citizenship to most free inhabitants of the empire, and for the monumental Baths of Caracalla in Rome. In 217, while campaigning in the East against Parthia, he was assassinated near Carrhae by a soldier, Justin Martialis, in a plot associated with the future emperor Macrinus.

Ibrahim I was the Ottoman sultan from 1640 to 1648, the son of Ahmed I and Kösem Sultan, and a ruler whose reign became associated with palace factionalism, financial strain, war pressure, and stories of unstable behavior. Known in later tradition as “Ibrahim the Mad,” he governed during a tense phase of Ottoman politics. In 1648, amid Janissary and religious-establishment revolt, he was deposed, confined in Topkapı Palace, and strangled on 18 August 1648, dying at 32.

His death quickly exposed tensions at court: rival factions backed his sons Edward and Æthelred, and the succession dispute helped unravel some of the order associated with his reign.

In 383, after losing support from his troops during the revolt of Magnus Maximus, he fled to Lugdunum (Lyon) and was murdered there at the age of 24.

Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Horst Wessel is highly controversial because he was an SA activist and became a major Nazi propaganda martyr. His lyrics became the Nazi Party anthem, and his image was deliberately used by Joseph Goebbels and the Nazi movement to glorify political violence and National Socialism.

Horst Wessel was a German SA activist whose name became inseparable from early Nazi propaganda. Born in Bielefeld in 1907, he joined radical nationalist circles and rose within the Sturmabteilung in Berlin, where Joseph Goebbels later turned him into one of the movement's best-known martyr figures. Wessel is chiefly remembered because lyrics he wrote were turned into the 'Horst-Wessel-Lied,' which became the Nazi Party anthem. In January 1930 he was shot in the head in Berlin during a violent dispute involving Communist opponents and a conflict connected to his lodgings and unpaid rent; after weeks of treatment, he died from complications of the wound on 23 February 1930 at the age of 22.

Why this is controversial: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim is a highly contested figure because he led the Umayyad conquest of Sindh and Multan, an armed expansion that involved invasion, regime change, and the beginning of long-term Muslim rule in parts of the Indian subcontinent. He is praised in some traditions as a capable young commander and criticized in others as a conqueror whose campaign brought violence, subjugation, and enduring religious-political conflict.

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim was the young Umayyad general whose conquest of Sindh and Multan created the first lasting Muslim foothold in the Indian subcontinent. Appointed in his teens, he combined speed, siege warfare and political bargaining to defeat Raja Dahir and establish Umayyad rule, becoming one of the most consequential commanders of the early 8th century. His rise ended suddenly after a change of caliph: recalled in 715 during court rivalries tied to al-Hajjaj's faction, he was imprisoned and died soon afterward in Iraq, most commonly said to be at Mosul.

Emperor Konoe

Birth date: June 15, 1139

Death date: August 21, 1155

Age: 16

Emperor Konoe was the 76th emperor of Japan, born in 1139 as a son of Emperor Toba and placed on the throne as a small child during the late Heian period, when real power remained with retired emperors and Fujiwara regents. His short reign sat at the center of fierce court rivalries that helped lead toward the Hōgen conflict. Frail for years and reportedly suffering severe eye trouble, he died at the Konoe Palace in 1155 at just 16, leaving no heir and triggering a dangerous succession crisis; afterward, rumors spread that he had been brought down by a curse.

Birth date: August 9, 1520

Death date: July 6, 1537

Age: 16

Madeleine of Valois was a French princess, the daughter of Francis I of France, who became Queen consort of Scotland in 1537 after marrying James V. Pavlik Morozov

Birth date: November 13, 1918

Death date: September 2, 1932

Age: 13
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Pavlik Morozov is highly controversial because Soviet authorities turned him into a Stalin-era propaganda symbol of loyalty to the state after he allegedly denounced his father during collectivization. Later historians have questioned major parts of the official story, and his legend remains associated with informing, family betrayal, state propaganda, and political martyr-making.

Pavel Trofimovich Morozov, known as Pavlik Morozov, was a Soviet peasant boy from Gerasimovka who became one of the most famous child figures of Stalin-era propaganda. He was celebrated across the USSR as a symbol of loyalty to the state after allegedly denouncing his father during collectivization; his story inspired books, songs, plays and monuments, even as later historians questioned parts of the official legend. In September 1932, at age 13, he was killed in his native village together with his younger brother, and his death was turned into a political martyr narrative.

Petr Ginz was a Czechoslovak Jewish diarist, writer, artist, and gifted young intellectual from Prague, known for his early novels, drawings, and for editing the boys’ magazine Vedem in the Theresienstadt ghetto. Age: 12

Childebert the Adopted, also known as Childebert III the Adopted, was a 7th-century Frankish king of Austrasia, probably born around 650 as the son of Grimoald the Elder. Adopted by King Sigebert III and raised as a rival heir, he was placed on the throne after Dagobert II was tonsured and exiled, making him one of the most striking figures in the Merovingian succession struggles. His rule ended when the political backlash against Grimoald’s coup caught up with him, and he was deposed and probably executed in 662.

Emperor Chūkyō was the 85th emperor of Japan, the son of Emperor Juntoku, and one of the most short-lived rulers in Japanese history. He died in 1234 at age 15 after years away from power, and the standard sources do not clearly record a cause of death.

Emperor Shijō was the 87th emperor of Japan, born in 1231 as the son of Emperor Go-Horikawa and placed on the throne as a small child during the Kamakura period. Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Herbert Norkus is highly controversial because he was a member of the Hitler Youth and became a major Nazi propaganda martyr after his death. His image was used to glorify Nazi youth activism, political violence, sacrifice for the movement, and loyalty to an extremist regime.

Herbert Norkus was a Berlin teenager and member of the Hitler Youth whose name became widely known after Nazi propagandists turned him into a martyr figure. Born into a working-class family, he joined the movement during the violent final years of the Weimar Republic. On 24 January 1932, while distributing Nazi leaflets in Berlin, he was chased and stabbed during a clash with communist youths, dying at age 15. His death was later heavily exploited in Nazi literature and film, especially through Hitler Youth Quex.

Anteo Zamboni was an Italian youth from Bologna, remembered as the alleged teenage attacker in one of the most dramatic attempts on Benito Mussolini’s life. Joseph Ferdinand Leopold of Bavaria was the Electoral Prince of Bavaria and, despite his very short life, one of the most important child dynasts in late 17th-century Europe. Yolande Louise of Savoy was a Savoyard princess, the daughter of Charles I, Duke of Savoy, and Blanche of Montferrat, who became Duchess of Savoy through her marriage to her cousin Philibert II. She died in Geneva on 12 September 1499 at just 12 years old, apparently without surviving children, and the standard references do not securely record a precise cause of death. Her body was associated with the dynastic burial tradition of Hautecombe Abbey, and her early death shifted those inheritance claims to collateral relatives.

David Vetter

Death date: February 21, 1984

Age: 12

David Phillip Vetter was an American child known worldwide as “the boy in the bubble” because he was born with severe combined immunodeficiency, a condition that left him unable to fight ordinary infections. To keep him alive, doctors raised him in sterile plastic isolators at Texas Children’s Hospital and later at home, making his life a landmark case in immunology, medical ethics, and public awareness of SCID. In 1983 he received a bone marrow transplant from his sister, but the procedure introduced Epstein-Barr virus, leading to lymphoma. He died in 1984 at the age of 12.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Emperor Houfei of Liu Song is highly controversial because historical accounts describe his reign as violent, arbitrary, and frightening even to his own court. Although he was very young, he is remembered as a ruler whose conduct helped trigger his assassination and posthumous demotion.

Liu Yu, better known as the Latter Deposed Emperor of Liu Song or Emperor Houfei, was a child ruler of China’s Liu Song dynasty who came to the throne in 472 after the death of his father, Emperor Ming. His brief reign became notorious for violent, arbitrary behavior and a court increasingly dominated by powerful officials. In 477, after frightening even his own protectors and threatening key figures around him, he was assassinated while asleep by the attendant Yang Yufu in a coup associated with Xiao Daocheng. He died at age 14 and was posthumously demoted to Prince of Cangwu.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Simon of Trent was a child and was not personally responsible for any wrongdoing. The controversy is about the posthumous cult and martyr narrative built around his death, which became a major anti-Jewish blood-libel case. Local Jews were falsely accused, tortured, and executed, and the story was used for centuries to promote antisemitic religious propaganda before the Catholic Church suppressed the cult in 1965.

Simon of Trent (Simonino di Trento) was a toddler from 15th-century Trent whose death became one of Europe’s most notorious blood-libel cases. After he disappeared during Easter week in 1475, his body was found a few days later; local Jews were falsely accused, tortured into confessions, and several were executed, while Simon’s cult spread for centuries before being suppressed by the Catholic Church in 1965.

Why this is controversial: Gabriel of Białystok is a highly sensitive figure because later religious narratives about his death became connected with antisemitic blood-libel accusations. Gabriel of Białystok, also known as Gabriel of Zabłudów or Gavriil Belostoksky, was a child from the village of Zwierki in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth who became venerated in Eastern Orthodoxy as a child martyr and patron of children. His cult grew after traditions about the discovery and transfer of his relics, and he was canonized in the 19th century. He died at the age of 6 near Białystok; later hagiography describes an abduction and killing, while modern writers note that the traditional accusation became entangled with antisemitic blood-libel claims.

Death date: June 21, 143

Cao E (曹娥) was a young Eastern Han girl from Shangyu, in today’s Shaoxing, Zhejiang, remembered as one of China’s classic models of filial devotion. In 143, aged about 13, she searched for her father after he drowned during a Dragon Boat Festival river rite and died in the river while trying to recover him.

Mary Scott, 3rd Countess of Buccleuch and Countess of Tarras, was a Scottish noblewoman who inherited the Buccleuch title as a child after the death of her father, Francis Scott. Elizabeth Cecilia “Lizzie” van Zyl was a South African Boer child whose photograph became one of the most haunting images associated with the British concentration camps of the Second Anglo-Boer War. Did you know:

For most of history, a drink of water was also a gamble. Rivers, wells, and town pumps could carry sewage-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In the United States, typhoid fever was about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900; after water treatment, sanitation, and disinfection spread, it fell to 33.8 by 1920 and 0.1 by 2006. A glass of boring tap water may be one of the greatest inventions in history.

The humbling part is that this is not ancient history everywhere. WHO estimates that around 1 million people still die each year from diarrhoea linked to unsafe drinking water, sanitation, and hand hygiene. So when someone in a modern city turns a tap, showers, brushes teeth, and flushes a toilet without thinking, they are living inside a public-health miracle.
